# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.

input.content: Ostrich 0.9 benchmark (project wiki https://wiki.example.com/ostrich-benchmark, March 2026): 4.1x average ratio on 2,000 text log files each under 1 MB (zstd level 3: 3.2x), 410 MB/s on one core. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs were not tested.
input.keywords: Ostrich, compression, benchmark, zstd, ratio, throughput, text logs

input.content: Ostrich README (https://ostrich.dev/readme, read 2026-10-27): Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records; it trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and the same dictionary is needed to decompress.
input.keywords: Ostrich, compressor, dictionary, ostrich train, decompress, small text records

final.result:
**Probably not, and the evidence we have can't show that it is.**

- **Different kind of data:** The README describes Ostrich as a dictionary compressor for *small text records*. Our archives are *protobuf binary frames, 40–300 MB per file* (telemetry-archives.md).
- **The benchmark doesn't apply:** The 4.1× result (vs. 3.2× for zstd level 3) at 410 MB/s came from text log files under 1 MB. The wiki says binary payloads and files over 1 MB weren't tested, so those numbers tell us nothing about our case.
- **It adds work:** Each stream needs its own trained dictionary (`ostrich train`), and you need that same dictionary to decompress. For long-term archives, that's one more thing to store and keep versioned alongside the data.

If you still want to consider it, run a test on a few real nightly files against zstd (try a higher level or `--long`) before deciding. Otherwise zstd is the safer default.

I saved what the wiki benchmark and the README say to the research shelf in memory, so a later look at this can start from there.
